entries.title: The 3,500 kcal per pound rule is a rough guide that varies with body fat
entries.take: About 3,500 kcal (7,700 per kg) per pound of loss is only an average, and leaner people need less per unit lost.
entries.body: The rule says a cumulative deficit of 3,500 kcal equals one pound (32.2 MJ per kg) of weight loss. A model found it approximately matches obese people with more than 30 kg of body fat, and it overestimates the deficit needed for people with less body fat. Weight also responds slowly: the half time was about one year in a separate model. Use it to size a plan, then correct against the scale.
do: Use the rule to pick a starting deficit, then check the trend over three to four weeks.

entries.title: Aim to lose about 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week
entries.take: A pace of 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week is the usual advice for keeping muscle while getting leaner.
entries.body: A contest-prep review recommends 0.5 to 1 percent a week, and a later review prefers 0.5 percent or less for attenuating fat-free mass loss. In 24 athletes, both groups lost about 5.5 percent of body weight, but the 0.7 percent weekly group gained 2.1 percent lean mass and lost 31 percent of fat mass, while the 1.4 percent group kept lean mass unchanged and lost 21 percent of fat mass. At 80 kg (176 lb), 0.5 to 1 percent is 0.4 to 0.8 kg (0.9 to 1.8 lb).
do: Pick a weekly percentage, convert it to kg or lb, and check against your four-week trend.

entries.title: Deficits much beyond 500 kcal a day cost lean mass in lifters
entries.take: In a meta-regression, a deficit of about 500 kcal a day stopped lean-mass gains from training, while strength held up.
entries.body: A systematic review and meta-analysis of resistance training in an energy deficit found lean-mass gains were impaired against training without a deficit (effect size -0.57), but strength gains were comparable. The meta-regression put the point where gains were prevented at roughly 500 kcal a day. For people trying to preserve lean mass rather than add it, the authors advise avoiding deficits above that size.
do: Keep deficits at or below about 500 kcal a day if gaining or keeping muscle is the priority.

entries.title: Eat more protein when you diet: about 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of lean mass
entries.take: Lean lifters in a deficit kept more muscle with higher protein, around 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass.
entries.body: A review of six studies in lean, resistance-trained athletes in a deficit put protein needs at 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of fat-free mass, scaled up with the severity of the deficit and the leanness. The ISSN position gives 2.3 to 3.1 g per kg of body weight. In a 4-week trial of 40 young men on a large deficit, 2.4 g/kg gained 1.2 kg of lean mass against 0.1 kg on 1.2 g/kg. A meta-analysis of 24 trials found higher protein held on to 0.43 kg more fat-free mass.
do: Set protein by your lean mass, and move up as the diet gets harder and you get leaner.

entries.title: Keep lifting while dieting, because training tells the body to keep muscle
entries.take: Resistance training reduced the lean mass lost in a diet, and strength was largely kept in deficit trials.
entries.body: An overview of 12 systematic reviews (149 studies) found resistance training limited lean mass loss during weight loss by about 0.8 kg. In six trials of older adults with obesity, training offset about 93 percent of the lean mass lost to calorie restriction. Strength gains in the deficit trials were comparable with and without a deficit.
do: Keep the main lifts heavy, and drop sets before you drop load.

entries.title: Short sleep shifts diet loss toward muscle and away from fat
entries.take: In ten adults, five and a half hours of sleep cut the fat share of weight lost by 55 percent.
entries.body: Ten overweight adults ate a reduced-calorie diet for 14 days in two conditions, with 8.5 or 5.5 hours in bed. Short sleep cut the fraction of weight lost as fat by 55 percent (1.4 vs 0.6 kg) and increased loss of fat-free mass by 60 percent (1.5 vs 2.4 kg). Hunger rose too. It is a very small and short crossover study, so treat it as a strong hint and not a finding.
do: Protect seven to nine hours in bed while dieting.

entries.title: Protein and unprocessed food help control hunger, at least in the short run
entries.take: Protein reduced hunger in meal studies, and a ward trial found unprocessed meals led to about 500 kcal less intake.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 49 acute studies found protein lowered hunger and raised fullness, but long-term trials were inconclusive. In a ward study of 20 adults, ultra-processed meals led to 508 kcal a day more intake than unprocessed meals matched on presented calories, sugar, fibre and sodium, with weight up 0.9 kg against down 0.9 kg over two weeks. That is one small, short crossover trial.
do: Build meals around protein and whole foods before cutting portion size.

entries.title: Appetite rises as you lose weight, so hunger is part of the process
entries.take: In one 52-week trial, appetite rose enough to add about 100 kcal a day per kg of weight lost.
entries.body: In 153 people losing weight without being aware of the deficit, a model found eating drifted above baseline by about 100 kcal a day for each kilogram lost, more than three times the matching fall in energy expenditure. This is one analysis of one drug trial. It points to appetite, not metabolism, as the main pressure against keeping weight off.
do: Plan for hunger to rise late in a diet, and use protein, fibre and a fixed end date.

entries.title: Metabolic slowdown with dieting is real but smaller than most people fear
entries.take: Adaptation is real but small, tens to low hundreds of kcal a day in most studies, so check your log first.
entries.body: A systematic review of 33 studies (2,528 participants) found adaptive thermogenesis in 27, with lower or non-significant values in the better-designed studies. In 171 women, the drop after loss was 54 kcal a day, and in a subset of 46 it was no longer significant at one and two years. In 32 men on a 50 percent deficit for three weeks, true adaptation was 72 kcal a day. After 6 years, 14 Biggest Loser contestants were 499 kcal a day below prediction, an extreme case.
do: Check the log and weekends before blaming metabolism.

entries.title: Day-to-day weight changes are mostly water, so read the trend
entries.take: Two-week changes of 1 to 3 kg were largely fat-free mass and water, not fat, in free-living adults.
entries.body: In 46 adults, a unit of two-week weight change was 84 percent fat-free mass, and the energy density of 1 to 3 kg changes was about 2,380 kcal per kg, well below that of fat. Glycogen is stored with three to four parts water. Weight runs higher on Sunday and Monday in 80 adults, and fluid retention peaks at the start of menstrual flow in 62 women. None of these is fat gain.
do: Weigh at the same time under the same conditions, and judge the weekly average.

entries.title: A two-week stall is not proof your diet stopped working
entries.take: Check logging and weekend intake before cutting calories, since stalls are usually noise or under-logging.
entries.body: Ten people who reported not losing weight on under 1,200 kcal actually under-reported intake by 47 percent and over-reported activity by 51 percent. In a one-year trial of 48 adults, calorie-restricted participants stopped losing weight on weekends. Add water noise from the table above and a two-week stall tells you little. A real stall holds over three to four weeks of honest logging.
do: Wait three to four weeks, then cut by about 100 to 200 kcal or add steps.

entries.title: Diet breaks and refeeds give mixed fat-loss results and may ease hunger
entries.take: Planned weeks at maintenance did not improve fat loss in lifters, and they lowered hunger.
entries.body: In 61 resistance-trained adults over 12 weeks, alternating three weeks of restriction with one week at maintenance gave the same fat and lean mass as continuous dieting, with lower hunger. A meta-analysis of 12 trials (881 participants) found the same body composition and a smaller drop in resting rate. A small 7-week trial found a weekly two-day carb refeed kept more lean mass (-0.4 vs -1.3 kg). Results in men with obesity favoured breaks.
do: Try a one-week break at maintenance if hunger or training quality is slipping.

entries.title: The best diet is the one you can keep to, since types differ little
entries.take: Low-carb and low-fat diets lost about the same weight, so pick the one you can keep.
entries.body: A network meta-analysis of 48 randomized trials (7,286 people) found weight loss with any low-carbohydrate or low-fat diet, with small differences among named diets. A larger analysis of 121 trials (21,942 patients) found about 4.6 kg at 6 months with low carb and 4.4 kg with low fat. In a 12-month trial of 609 adults, the difference was 0.7 kg, not significant. Behavioural support added about 3.2 kg at six months in one analysis.
do: Choose the pattern that fits your food preferences and schedule.

entries.title: Intermittent fasting works by eating less, with no clear extra effect
entries.take: Time-restricted eating did not beat plain calorie control in long trials, though one pooled analysis disagrees.
entries.body: In 139 adults over 12 months, eating 8 am to 4 pm with calorie restriction lost 8.0 kg against 6.3 kg for calorie restriction alone, not a significant difference. A 12-week trial of 116 people found no advantage, and a 41-person feeding trial matched calories and found no effect on weight. A pooled analysis of 30 studies did report 1.46 kg more loss in matched comparisons. With lifting, an analysis of eight studies (221 participants) kept fat-free mass.
do: Use a fasting window only if it makes eating less easier for you.

entries.title: Meal frequency and late eating matter little for fat loss at equal calories
entries.take: Differences between meal patterns are small at equal calories; fewer meals showed about 1 kg more loss in one analysis.
entries.body: A network meta-analysis of 22 trials (647 people) found two meals a day slightly lowered weight against three meals or six, by about 1 kg, under equal calories. In 16 obese adults on the same deficit, three meals and three snacks did no better than three meals. A meta-analysis of 9 trials found earlier eating gave 1.2 kg more loss, and a controlled crossover trial found late eating raised hunger. Pick the pattern you can follow.
do: Choose a meal pattern around your day, and keep protein in each meal.

entries.title: Exercise adds to fat loss, and daily movement drops on diets if you let it
entries.take: Exercise adds 1.5 to 3.5 kg of loss in reviews, and people on diets may move less outside the gym.
entries.body: An overview of 12 meta-analyses found exercise led to 1.5 to 3.5 kg of weight loss and similar results from aerobic and interval training when energy expenditure matched. The ACSM suggests 150 minutes a week as a floor and 200 to 300 for long-term loss. A systematic review of 36 articles found lower non-exercise activity in 63 percent of diet-only arms. In 16 overfed adults, NEAT explained the large differences in fat gain.
do: Set a daily step or activity floor and keep it during the diet.

entries.title: Getting very lean costs hormones, mood and training quality, so go carefully
entries.take: Prolonged energy availability under about 25 kcal per kg of lean mass led to muscle loss and hormonal and mood problems.
entries.body: Reviews of lean athletes link a long period at low energy availability to muscle loss, hormone disruption and psychological problems. A case study of one natural bodybuilder saw body fat fall from 14.8 to 4.5 percent and testosterone from 9.22 to 2.27 ng/mL, recovering after the contest. In 27 women dieting for a fitness show, sex hormones fell and menstrual irregularities rose, and most recovered within three to four months. Involve a coach and clinician.
do: Treat contest-level leanness as a short, supervised project, not a lifestyle.
See a clinician if periods stop or mood drops.

entries.title: Weight regain is common, and maintenance is possible with sustained habits
entries.take: Most people regain some weight, and a minority keep most of it off by staying active and weighing themselves.
entries.body: In 171 women, participants regained 52 percent of the weight lost at one year and 89 percent at two. A meta-analysis of 29 US studies found that after five years the average person kept off more than 3 kg. Among 2,886 National Weight Control Registry members, mean loss was 31.3 kg at entry and 23.1 kg at ten years. They report about an hour of activity a day, regular weighing and consistent eating on weekends. The registry is self-selected.
do: After the diet, raise calories in steps and keep weighing weekly.
Keep activity and protein high.

entries.title: A small surplus adds muscle, and a large surplus mostly adds fat
entries.take: A surplus of about 10 to 20 percent over maintenance is a common starting range for lifters, and nobody has proven the best size.
entries.body: A narrative review for physique athletes suggests 10 to 20 percent above maintenance, with advanced lifters more conservative. In 17 lifters over 8 weeks, a 15 percent surplus mainly increased fat gain rather than strength or muscle thickness. Another review finds the ideal surplus is unknown. If maintenance is 2,500 kcal, 10 to 20 percent is 250 to 500 kcal. Evidence is thin and short.
do: Start near the low end of the surplus and adjust to the scale.

entries.title: Recomposition works best for beginners, returners and people carrying more fat
entries.take: Gaining muscle while losing fat is realistic with high protein and hard training, and likely harder for lean, advanced lifters.
entries.body: In 40 young men on a roughly 40 percent deficit with heavy training and 2.4 g/kg of protein, lean mass rose 1.2 kg while fat mass fell 4.8 kg over four weeks. A review of six studies found that the groups that held on to or gained lean mass were among those with the highest body fat, the smallest deficit or a new training stimulus. Advanced lifters with low body fat have less room.
do: Use a small deficit or maintenance with high protein and progressive training.

entries.title: Cutting calories after a short stall
entries.take: Short stalls are mostly water and weekend noise, and cutting on them stacks deficit on top of a working plan.
entries.body: A two-week plateau can come from water, a missed weekend or logging drift, as 48 adults who stopped losing on weekends showed. Cutting calories on a stall moves you toward the 500 kcal limit sooner. Wait three to four weeks, check the log, and only then change calories or steps.
do: Check the four-week trend and the log before changing calories.

entries.title: Dieting faster than 1 percent of body weight a week
entries.take: Faster loss retained less lean mass in athletes, and the speed is hard to keep up.
entries.body: In 24 athletes, a 1.4 percent weekly loss kept lean mass unchanged and cut fat mass 21 percent, while a 0.7 percent loss gained 2.1 percent lean mass and cut fat mass 31 percent. Reviews recommend 0.5 to 1 percent a week.
do: Slow the deficit to 0.5 to 1 percent of body weight a week.

entries.title: Cutting protein and stopping lifting while dieting
entries.take: The two habits that protect muscle in a deficit are protein and heavy training, and dropping both costs lean mass.
entries.body: Higher protein held on to lean mass in trials of lean lifters, and training reduced lean loss by about 0.8 kg across an overview of reviews.
do: Keep protein high and lifts heavy until the diet ends.

entries.title: Treating a gaining phase as a licence to eat anything
entries.take: A large surplus mainly added fat in a trial, and extra fat has to be dieted off later.
entries.body: In 17 lifters, a 15 percent surplus mostly increased fat gain rather than strength or muscle thickness. A review suggests 10 to 20 percent for physique athletes, less for advanced lifters. The extra fat then has to be dieted off.
do: Use a measured surplus and watch the rate of weight gain.

entries.title: Dieting with no end date and no plan for after
entries.take: Regain follows the diet for most people, and a plan for the exit matters as much as the deficit.
entries.body: In 171 women, 52 percent of lost weight was regained after one year and 89 percent after two. Registry members who kept it off kept activity, regular weighing and steady eating. Set an end date for the diet.
do: Plan the exit: a target date, a maintenance range and a weekly weigh-in.
Step calories up toward maintenance over several weeks.

entries.title: Rate of loss
entries.take: Usual pace for keeping muscle; at 80 kg (176 lb) that is 0.4 to 0.8 kg a week.

entries.title: Deficit that stopped lean-mass gains
entries.take: In a meta-regression, deficits around this size prevented gains in lean mass in trained lifters.

entries.title: Protein in a deficit
entries.take: ISSN and review ranges for lean lifters dieting; raise it as the deficit and leanness grow.

entries.title: Energy per pound of weight lost
entries.take: The classic rule of thumb, which equals about 7,700 kcal per kg and varies with body fat.

entries.title: Energy per kg for short-term changes
entries.take: Two-week changes of 1 to 3 kg were mostly fat-free mass and water, so they carry less energy than fat.

entries.title: Appetite rise per kg of weight lost
entries.take: In one trial, eating drifted above baseline by about this much for each kilogram lost.

entries.title: Surplus for a gaining phase
entries.take: Suggested range for novice and intermediate lifters in a physique-sport review; advanced lifters go lower.

entries.title: Rate of gain, novice to intermediate
entries.take: At 80 kg (176 lb) that is 0.2 to 0.4 kg (0.4 to 0.9 lb) a week.

entries.title: Energy deficit
entries.take: Eating less energy than you use. It is the one requirement for losing body fat. A daily deficit of 500 kcal is about 3,500 kcal a week.

entries.title: Adaptive thermogenesis (metabolic adaptation)
entries.take: A fall in energy use beyond what the loss of body mass explains, seen during and after weight loss. Studies find it ranges from small to modest.

entries.title: NEAT (non-exercise activity)
entries.take: Non-exercise activity thermogenesis: energy spent on walking, standing, fidgeting and chores. It can fall during a diet without you noticing.

entries.title: Diet break and refeed
entries.take: A diet break is a planned stretch, often one to two weeks, at maintenance calories. A refeed is shorter, usually one or two days of higher carbohydrate.

entries.title: Recomposition
entries.take: Gaining muscle and losing fat at the same time, so body weight changes little while the body changes shape.

entries.title: Time-restricted eating
entries.take: Eating all meals within a set daily window, such as eight hours, and fasting for the rest. It is one form of intermittent fasting.

entries.title: Deficit size versus expected weekly loss
entries.take: Approximate weekly loss for a daily deficit at 7,700 kcal per kg (3,500 per lb), for an 80 kg (176 lb) person. It overstates loss for lean people.
rows: In range; near the limit seen for lean-mass trials
In range; hold protein and training high
Above 1%; more lean loss in athletes

entries.title: Rate of gain by training age
entries.take: Suggested pace of weight gain in a gaining phase; the research is thin and the rates are conservative.
rows: Mostly extra fat in an 8-week trial

entries.title: What moves scale weight day to day
entries.take: Short-term causes of scale changes that are not fat gain or loss.
rows: Each gram of glycogen is stored with three to four parts water
Weight is higher on Sunday and Monday, then falls
Fluid retention scores peak on the first day of flow
1-3 kg over two weeks is about 84% fat-free mass and water
Slow; about 0.5-1% of body weight a week at best

hall-2007.title: What is the required energy deficit per unit weight loss?
hall-2007.support: The rule of thumb approximately matches the predicted energy density of lost weight in obese subjects with an initial body fat above 30 kg but overestimates the cumulative energy deficit required per unit weight loss for people with lower initial body fat.

hall-2011.title: Quantification of the effect of energy imbalance on bodyweight
hall-2011.support: The bodyweight response to a change of energy intake is slow, with half times of about 1 year; adults with greater adiposity have a larger expected weight loss for the same change of energy intake.

helms-2014-prep.title: Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation
helms-2014-prep.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
helms-2014-prep.support: Caloric intake should be set at a level that results in bodyweight losses of approximately 0.5 to 1%/wk to maximize muscle retention; 2.3-3.1 g/kg of lean body mass of protein.

garthe-2011.title: Effect of Two Different Weight-Loss Rates on Body Composition and Strength and Power-Related Performance in Elite Athletes
garthe-2011.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
garthe-2011.support: 24 athletes; 0.7% vs 1.4% weekly loss; LBM increased 2.1% in the slow group and was unchanged (-0.2%) in the fast group.

roberts-2020.title: Nutritional Recommendations for Physique Athletes
roberts-2020.support: Slower rates of weight loss (<=0.5% of body mass per week) are preferable for attenuating the loss of fat-free mass, with diet breaks and refeeds possibly beneficial.

murphy-2021.title: Energy deficiency impairs resistance training gains in lean mass but not strength: A meta‐analysis and meta‐regression
murphy-2021.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
murphy-2021.support: Meta-regression: an energy deficit of ~500 kcal/day prevented gains in lean mass; strength gains were comparable between conditions.

helms-2014-protein.title: A Systematic Review of Dietary Protein During Caloric Restriction in Resistance Trained Lean Athletes: A Case for Higher Intakes
helms-2014-protein.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
helms-2014-protein.support: Six studies; protein needs for energy-restricted resistance-trained athletes are likely 2.3-3.1 g/kg of FFM scaled upwards with severity of caloric restriction and leanness.

jager-2017.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise
jager-2017.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
jager-2017.support: Higher protein intakes (2.3-3.1 g/kg/d) may be needed to maximize the retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained subjects during hypocaloric periods.

longland-2016.title: Higher compared with lower dietary protein during an energy deficit combined with intense exercise promotes greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss: a randomized trial
longland-2016.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
longland-2016.support: 40 young men, 4 weeks at about 40% energy deficit with resistance and interval training; 2.4 vs 1.2 g/kg protein: lean mass +1.2 vs +0.1 kg, fat mass -4.8 vs -3.5 kg.

wycherley-2012.title: Effects of energy-restricted high-protein, low-fat compared with standard-protein, low-fat diets: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
wycherley-2012.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
wycherley-2012.support: 24 trials with 1063 individuals; high-protein diets mitigated reductions in fat-free mass (0.43 kg) and resting energy expenditure.

sardeli-2018.title: Resistance Training Prevents Muscle Loss Induced by Caloric Restriction in Obese Elderly Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sardeli-2018.support: Six RCTs in obese elderly individuals; resistance training reduced 93.5% of calorie-restriction-induced lean body mass loss.

bellicha-2021.title: Effect of exercise training on weight loss, body composition changes, and weight maintenance in adults with overweight or obesity: An overview of 12 systematic reviews and 149 studies
bellicha-2021.support: Overview of 12 systematic reviews (149 studies); exercise led to weight loss of 1.5-3.5 kg; resistance training reduced lean mass loss during weight loss; no difference between aerobic and HIIT when energy expenditure is equal.

nedeltcheva-2010.title: Insufficient Sleep Undermines Dietary Efforts to Reduce Adiposity
nedeltcheva-2010.support: 10 overweight adults, 14 days of caloric restriction with 8.5 or 5.5 h of sleep opportunity; sleep curtailment decreased the proportion of weight lost as fat by 55% and increased loss of fat-free mass by 60%.

hall-2019.title: Ultra-Processed Diets Cause Excess Calorie Intake and Weight Gain: An Inpatient Randomized Controlled Trial of Ad Libitum Food Intake
hall-2019.support: 20 weight-stable adults in a ward; energy intake was greater on the ultra-processed diet by 508 kcal/day; +0.9 kg vs -0.9 kg over 2 weeks.

kohanmoo-2020.title: Effect of short- and long-term protein consumption on appetite and appetite-regulating gastrointestinal hormones, a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
kohanmoo-2020.support: 49 acute and 19 long-term publications; acute protein ingestion suppresses appetite; results of long-term trials are inconclusive.

polidori-2016.title: How Strongly Does Appetite Counter Weight Loss? Quantification of the Feedback Control of Human Energy Intake
polidori-2016.support: 153 patients in a 52-week trial; weight loss led to a proportional increase in appetite, eating above baseline by about 100 kcal/day per kilogram of lost weight.

peos-2021.title: Continuous versus Intermittent Dieting for Fat Loss and Fat-Free Mass Retention in Resistance-trained Adults: The ICECAP Trial
peos-2021.support: 61 resistance-trained adults over 12 weeks; no difference in fat mass or fat-free mass between intermittent and continuous restriction; the intermittent group had lower hunger.

campbell-2020.title: Intermittent Energy Restriction Attenuates the Loss of Fat Free Mass in Resistance Trained Individuals. A Randomized Controlled Trial
campbell-2020.journal: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
campbell-2020.support: 27 resistance-trained adults over 7 weeks; the two-day carbohydrate refeed group kept fat-free mass (-0.4 kg vs -1.3 kg) and resting metabolic rate better than the continuous group.

byrne-2018.title: Intermittent energy restriction improves weight loss efficiency in obese men: the MATADOR study
byrne-2018.support: 51 men with obesity; intermittent restriction gave greater weight loss (14.1 vs 9.1 kg) and fat loss than continuous restriction over the same 16 weeks of restriction.

poon-2024.title: Effects of intermittent dieting with break periods on body composition and metabolic adaptation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
poon-2024.support: 12 randomized trials with 881 participants; no group differences in body mass or fat loss; resting metabolic rate fell less after intermittent dieting with breaks.

nunes-cl-2021.title: Does adaptive thermogenesis occur after weight loss in adults? A systematic review
nunes-cl-2021.support: 33 studies with 2528 participants; adaptive thermogenesis observed in 27; well-designed studies reported lower or non-significant values.

martins-2020.title: Metabolic adaptation is not a major barrier to weight-loss maintenance
martins-2020.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
martins-2020.support: 171 overweight women followed 2 years; metabolic adaptation -54 kcal/d after loss and not significant at 1 or 2 years; participants regained 52% and 89% of weight lost at 1 and 2 years.

muller-2015.title: Metabolic adaptation to caloric restriction and subsequent refeeding: the Minnesota Starvation Experiment revisited
muller-2015.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
muller-2015.support: 32 nonobese men; 3 weeks at -50% of energy needs; adaptive thermogenesis 108 kcal/d, of which 72 kcal/d was true adaptive thermogenesis.

fothergill-2016.title: Persistent metabolic adaptation 6 years after “The Biggest Loser” competition
fothergill-2016.support: 14 Biggest Loser participants; at 6 years RMR was 704 kcal/day below baseline and metabolic adaptation was -499 kcal/day.

bhutani-2017.title: Composition of two-week change in body weight under unrestricted free-living conditions
bhutani-2017.support: 46 adults; two-week free-living weight changes were largely fat-free mass and water: 84% of a unit change in weight was fat-free mass; energy density of 1-3 kg changes averaged 2380 kcal/kg.

orsama-2014.title: Weight Rhythms: Weight Increases during Weekends and Decreases during Weekdays
orsama-2014.support: 80 adults, 4,657 measurements; higher weight early in the week (Sunday and Monday), decreasing during the week.

kreitzman-1992.title: Glycogen storage: illusions of easy weight loss, excessive weight regain, and distortions in estimates of body composition
kreitzman-1992.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
kreitzman-1992.support: Glycogen is stored in hydrated form (three to four parts water); changes in total body potassium in 11 subjects after 4 days on a very-low-calorie diet reflected glycogen mobilization.

white-2011.title: Fluid Retention over the Menstrual Cycle: 1-Year Data from the Prospective Ovulation Cohort
white-2011.support: 765 menstrual cycles in 62 healthy women; fluid retention scores peaked on the first day of menstrual flow and were lowest in the mid-follicular period.

lichtman-1992.title: Discrepancy between Self-Reported and Actual Caloric Intake and Exercise in Obese Subjects
lichtman-1992.support: Subjects reporting diet resistance under-reported actual food intake by 47 percent and over-reported physical activity by 51 percent.

authors: Washington University School of Medicine CALERIE Team
racette-2008.title: Influence of Weekend Lifestyle Patterns on Body Weight
racette-2008.support: 48 adults; on weekends calorie-restricted participants stopped losing weight.

johnston-2014.title: Comparison of Weight Loss Among Named Diet Programs in Overweight and Obese Adults
johnston-2014.support: 59 articles reporting 48 randomized trials (7286 individuals); significant weight loss with any low-carbohydrate or low-fat diet; differences between named diets were small.

ge-2020.title: Comparison of dietary macronutrient patterns of 14 popular named dietary programmes for weight and cardiovascular risk factor reduction in adults: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials
ge-2020.support: 121 eligible trials with 21,942 patients; low carbohydrate and low fat diets had a similar effect at six months on weight loss (4.63 vs 4.37 kg).

gardner-2018.title: Effect of Low-Fat vs Low-Carbohydrate Diet on 12-Month Weight Loss in Overweight Adults and the Association With Genotype Pattern or Insulin Secretion
gardner-2018.support: 609 adults; weight change at 12 months was -5.3 kg for low-fat vs -6.0 kg for low-carbohydrate (difference 0.7 kg, 95% CI -0.2 to 1.6).

liu-2022.title: Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss
liu-2022.support: 139 patients with obesity; 12 months; weight loss -8.0 kg with time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction vs -6.3 kg with calorie restriction alone (not significantly different).

lowe-2020.title: Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity
lowe-2020.support: 116 participants, 12 weeks; time-restricted eating was not more effective for weight loss than eating throughout the day.

maruthur-2024.title: Effect of Isocaloric, Time-Restricted Eating on Body Weight in Adults With Obesity
maruthur-2024.support: 41 adults, isocaloric feeding for 12 weeks; weight decreased 2.3 kg with time-restricted eating and 2.6 kg with usual eating; any effect in earlier studies may be due to lower calorie intake.

fernandes-2025.title: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials Comparing Time-Restricted Eating With and Without Caloric Restriction for Weight Loss
fernandes-2025.support: 30 studies, 1341 participants; time-restricted eating reduced body weight even in isocaloric comparisons (-1.46 kg).

keenan-2020.title: The Effects of Intermittent Fasting Combined with Resistance Training on Lean Body Mass: A Systematic Review of Human Studies
keenan-2020.support: Eight studies; intermittent fasting paired with resistance training generally maintains LBM and can promote fat loss.

ashtary-2021.title: Effects of intermittent fasting combined with resistance training on body composition: a systematic review and meta‐analysis
ashtary-2021.support: Eight studies including 221 participants; intermittent fasting plus resistance training reduced fat mass by 1.36 kg relative to non-IF diets without a significant effect on fat-free mass.

schwingshackl-2020.title: Impact of Meal Frequency on Anthropometric Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
schwingshackl-2020.support: 22 RCTs with 647 participants; two meals a day probably slightly reduces body weight compared with three (-1.02 kg) or six meals (-1.29 kg) under isocaloric conditions.

cameron-2010.title: Increased meal frequency does not promote greater weight loss in subjects who were prescribed an 8-week equi-energetic energy-restricted diet
cameron-2010.support: 16 obese adults, 8 weeks at the same energy restriction; no differences in weight loss, appetite or gut peptides between 3 meals plus 3 snacks and 3 meals a day.

young-2022.title: Distribution of energy intake across the day and weight loss: A systematic review and meta‐analysis
young-2022.support: Nine RCTs; in an energy-reduced diet, earlier distribution of intake gave greater weight loss (-1.23 kg; 95% CI -2.40 to -0.06).

vujovic-2022.title: Late isocaloric eating increases hunger, decreases energy expenditure, and modifies metabolic pathways in adults with overweight and obesity
vujovic-2022.support: Randomized crossover trial; late eating increased hunger and decreased waketime energy expenditure with nutrient intake, activity, sleep and light controlled.

donnelly-2009.title: Appropriate Physical Activity Intervention Strategies for Weight Loss and Prevention of Weight Regain for Adults
donnelly-2009.support: A minimum of 150 min/wk of moderate-intensity physical activity for overweight adults; 200-300 min/wk recommended for long-term weight loss.

silva-2018.title: What is the effect of diet and/or exercise interventions on behavioural compensation in non-exercise physical activity and related energy expenditure of free-living adults? A systematic review
silva-2018.support: 36 articles, 1561 participants; compensation (lower NEAT or NEPA) observed in 26 of 70 arms, representing 63% of diet-only, 27% of combined and 23% of exercise-only arms.

levine-1999.title: Role of Nonexercise Activity Thermogenesis in Resistance to Fat Gain in Humans
levine-1999.support: 16 nonobese volunteers overfed by 1000 kcal/day for 8 weeks; changes in NEAT accounted for the 10-fold differences in fat storage.

fagerberg-2018.title: Negative Consequences of Low Energy Availability in Natural Male Bodybuilding: A Review
fagerberg-2018.journal: International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism
fagerberg-2018.support: A prolonged energy availability under 25 kcal/kg FFM results in muscle loss, hormonal imbalances and psychological problems; a more tempered approach (>25 kcal/kg FFM) might result in less muscle loss.

rossow-2013.title: Natural Bodybuilding Competition Preparation and Recovery: A 12-Month Case Study
rossow-2013.journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
rossow-2013.support: Case study of one natural bodybuilder; body fat fell from 14.8% to 4.5% and testosterone from 9.22 to 2.27 ng/mL during preparation, returning to baseline after competition.

hulmi-2017.title: The Effects of Intensive Weight Reduction on Body Composition and Serum Hormones in Female Fitness Competitors
hulmi-2017.support: 27 dieting women and 23 controls; ~12% body weight loss over 4 months; hormones including leptin, T3, testosterone and estradiol fell and menstrual irregularities increased; most recovered within 3-4 months.

loucks-2003.title: Luteinizing Hormone Pulsatility Is Disrupted at a Threshold of Energy Availability in Regularly Menstruating Women
loucks-2003.journal: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
loucks-2003.support: 29 young women; luteinizing hormone pulsatility was unaffected at 30 kcal/kg LBM/day of energy availability, and disrupted below this threshold.

mountjoy-2023.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee’s (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)
mountjoy-2023.support: 2023 IOC consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport; health and performance outcomes of low energy availability in female and male athletes.

thomas-jg-2014.title: Weight-Loss Maintenance for 10 Years in the National Weight Control Registry
thomas-jg-2014.support: 2886 National Weight Control Registry participants; mean loss 31.3 kg at entry, 23.8 kg at 5 years and 23.1 kg at 10 years; more than 87% still maintaining at least a 10% loss at years 5 and 10.

wing-2005.title: Long-term weight loss maintenance
wing-2005.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
wing-2005.support: Members have lost an average of 33 kg and maintained the loss for more than 5 y, with about 1 h/d of physical activity, self-monitoring of weight and a consistent eating pattern across weekdays and weekends.

anderson-2001.title: Long-term weight-loss maintenance: a meta-analysis of US studies
anderson-2001.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
anderson-2001.support: 29 US studies; 5 years after structured weight-loss programs the average individual maintained a weight loss of >3 kg and a reduced weight of >3%.

rosenbaum-2010.title: Adaptive thermogenesis in humans
rosenbaum-2010.support: Over 80% of people return to pre-weight-loss body fatness after otherwise successful weight loss; adaptive thermogenesis is operant in lean and obese individuals.

iraki-2019.title: Nutrition Recommendations for Bodybuilders in the Off-Season: A Narrative Review
iraki-2019.support: A hyper-energetic diet (~10-20%) with a target weight gain of ~0.25-0.5% of body weight per week for novice/intermediate bodybuilders; advanced bodybuilders should be more conservative.

helms-2023.title: Effect of Small and Large Energy Surpluses on Strength, Muscle, and Skinfold Thickness in Resistance-Trained Individuals: A Parallel Groups Design
helms-2023.support: 21 trained lifters randomized, 17 completers over 8 weeks; maintenance vs 5% vs 15% energy surplus; faster rates of body mass gain primarily increase rates of fat gain rather than augmenting strength or muscle thickness.

slater-2019.title: Is an Energy Surplus Required to Maximize Skeletal Muscle Hypertrophy Associated With Resistance Training
slater-2019.support: The specific energy surplus required to facilitate muscle hypertrophy is unknown; there is clear evidence of an anabolic stimulus from an energy surplus.

helms-2019.title: Towards a Sustainable Nutrition Paradigm in Physique Sport: A Narrative Review
helms-2019.support: Physique athletes have higher body image and eating disorder rates; best-practice suggestions include dietary flexibility and slower weight loss.

hall-kahan-2018.title: Maintenance of Lost Weight and Long-Term Management of Obesity
hall-kahan-2018.support: Obesity interventions typically result in early weight loss followed by a weight plateau and progressive regain.
